61	    # Render two user turns that differ only in body text; the shared trailing run is the separator.
62	    # A bare string ``content`` is rejected by some multimodal processors (they iterate ``content``
63	    # expecting a list of typed parts), so fall back to the list-of-parts form, and return ``[]`` if
64	    # neither renders. Both probes must use the same form so only the body differs.
65	    empty = filled = None
66	    for as_parts in (False, True):
67	        if as_parts:
68	            body_empty, body_filled = [{"type": "text", "text": ""}], [{"type": "text", "text": "x"}]
69	        else:
70	            body_empty, body_filled = "", "x"
71	        try:
72	            empty = normalize_token_ids(
73	                tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
74	                    [{"role": "user", "content": body_empty}],
75	                    add_generation_prompt=False,
76	                    tokenize=True,
77	                    **apply_chat_template_kwargs,
78	                )
79	            )
80	            filled = normalize_token_ids(
81	                tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
82	                    [{"role": "user", "content": body_filled}],
83	                    add_generation_prompt=False,
84	                    tokenize=True,
85	                    **apply_chat_template_kwargs,
86	                )
87	            )
88	            break
89	        except Exception:
90	            empty = filled = None
91	    if empty is None or filled is None:
92	        return []
93	    # Maximal common trailing run == the message closing token(s) + inter-turn separator (identical
94	    # regardless of content).
95	    i = 0
96	    while i < len(empty) and i < len(filled) and empty[-1 - i] == filled[-1 - i]:
97	        i += 1
98	    suffix = empty[len(empty) - i :]
99	    if not suffix:
100	        return []
101	    # Split off the closing token the model already emits; the remainder is the dropped separator.
102	    # A processor (VLM path) exposes ``eos_token_id`` on its wrapped tokenizer rather than itself,
103	    # and some tokenizers (e.g. Llama 3) expose it as a list/tuple of ids rather than a single int.
104	    eos_id = getattr(tokenizer, "eos_token_id", None)
105	    if eos_id is None:
106	        eos_id = getattr(getattr(tokenizer, "tokenizer", None), "eos_token_id", None)
107	    eos_ids = {eos_id} if isinstance(eos_id, int) else set(eos_id or [])
108	    last_close = max((i for i, tok_id in enumerate(suffix) if tok_id in eos_ids), default=None)
109	    if last_close is not None:
110	        return suffix[last_close + 1 :]
111	    return suffix[1:]
112	
113	
114	def extract_system_prompt_and_generation(tokenizer, **apply_chat_template_kwargs):
115	    token1 = normalize_token_ids(
116	        tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
117	            [{"role": "user", "content": ""}], add_generation_prompt=False, tokenize=True, **apply_chat_template_kwargs
118	        )
119	    )
120	    token2 = normalize_token_ids(
121	        tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
122	            [{"role": "user", "content": ""}] * 2,
123	            add_generation_prompt=False,
124	            tokenize=True,
125	            **apply_chat_template_kwargs,
126	        )
127	    )
128	    # get system prompt tokens
129	    system_prompt = token1[: -(len(token2) - len(token1))]
130	    # get generate prompt tokens
131	    token3 = normalize_token_ids(
132	        tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
133	            [{"role": "user", "content": ""}], add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, **apply_chat_template_kwargs
134	        )
135	    )
136	    generate_prompt = token3[len(token1) :]
137	
138	    return system_prompt, generate_prompt
139	
140	
141	def apply_chat_template(
142	    processor: PreTrainedTokenizerBase | ProcessorMixin,
143	    messages: list[dict],
144	    *,
145	    tokenize: bool = True,
146	    add_generation_prompt: bool = True,
147	    tools=None,
148	    return_dict: bool = False,
149	    **kwargs,
150	) -> list[int] | str:
151	    """apply_chat_template to messages with special attention to template requiring
152	    at least one user message, e.g. Qwen3.5.
153	
154	    Args:
155	        processor: tokenizer or processor.
156	        messages: list[dict], messages.
157	        tokenize: bool, whether to tokenize the output.
158	        add_generation_prompt: bool, whether to add generation prompt.
159	        tools: list[dict], tools schema.
160	        return_dict: bool, whether to return a dict.
161	        **kwargs: additional arguments for apply_chat_template.
162	
163	    Returns:
164	        list[int] | str: tokenized ids or text string.
165	    """
166	    try:
167	        return processor.apply_chat_template(
168	            messages,
169	            tokenize=tokenize,
170	            add_generation_prompt=add_generation_prompt,
171	            tools=tools,
172	            return_dict=return_dict,
173	            **kwargs,
174	        )
175	    except Exception:
176	        # Qwen3.5 apply_chat_template needs messages with at least one user message
177	        dummy_user_message = [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": ""}]}]
178	        dummy_user_prefix = processor.apply_chat_template(
179	            dummy_user_message,
180	            tokenize=tokenize,
181	            add_generation_prompt=False,
182	            tools=tools,
183	            return_dict=return_dict,
184	            **kwargs,
185	        )
186	        output = processor.apply_chat_template(
187	            dummy_user_message + messages,
188	            tokenize=tokenize,
189	            add_generation_prompt=add_generation_prompt,
190	            tools=tools,
191	            return_dict=return_dict,
192	            **kwargs,
193	        )
194	
195	        if not tokenize:  # tokenize=False
196	            return output[len(dummy_user_prefix) :]
197	        elif not return_dict:  # tokenize=True and return_dict=False
198	            if isinstance(output[0], list):  # transformers>=5
199	                assert len(output) == 1, "output must be a list[int] or list[list[int]]"
200	                dummy_user_prefix = dummy_user_prefix[0]
201	                output = output[0]
202	            return output[len(dummy_user_prefix) :]
203	        else:  # tokenize=True and return_dict=True and return_tensors="pt"
204	            dummy_user_prefix = dict(dummy_user_prefix)
205	            output = dict(output)
206	            prefix_len = dummy_user_prefix["input_ids"].shape[1]
207	            output["input_ids"] = output["input_ids"][:, prefix_len:]
208	            output["attention_mask"] = output["attention_mask"][:, prefix_len:]
209	            if "mm_token_type_ids" in output:
210	                output["mm_token_type_ids"] = output["mm_token_type_ids"][:, prefix_len:]
211	            return output

299	    def _build_messages(self, example: dict, key: str):
300	        """Replace multimodal placeholders in messages with structured content.
301	
302	        This is required by processor.apply_chat_template.
303	        - <image>: {"type": "image", "image": image} or {"type": "image", **image}
304	        - <video>: {"type": "video", "video": video} or {"type": "video", **video}
305	        - <audio>: {"type": "audio", "audio": audio} or {"type": "audio", **audio}
306	
307	        Args:
308	            example: Row dictionary from dataframe.
309	
310	        Returns:
311	            messages: List of messages with replaced placeholder.
312	        """
313	        messages: list = example[key]
314	        # When concatenating multimodal datasets, get will return None for samples without a modality column.
315	        images = example.get(self.image_key, None) or []
316	        videos = example.get(self.video_key, None) or []
317	        audios = example.get(self.audio_key, None) or []
318	
319	        image_offset, video_offset, audio_offset = 0, 0, 0
320	        for message in messages:
321	            if not images and not videos and not audios:
322	                continue
323	            assert self.processor is not None, "processor is needed to process multimodal data"
324	
325	            content = message["content"]
326	            if not isinstance(content, str):
327	                continue
328	
329	            content_list = []
330	            segments = re.split("(<image>|<video>|<audio>)", content)
331	            segments = [item for item in segments if item != ""]
332	            for segment in segments:
333	                if segment == "<image>":
334	                    assert image_offset < len(images), f"image_offset {image_offset} >= len(images) {len(images)}"
335	                    image = images[image_offset]
336	                    if isinstance(image, Image.Image):
337	                        image = image.convert("RGB")
338	                        content_list.append({"type": "image", "image": image})
339	                    elif isinstance(image, dict):
340	                        if "bytes" in image:
341	                            image["image"] = Image.open(BytesIO(image["bytes"]))
342	                        content_list.append({"type": "image", **image})
343	                    elif isinstance(image, str | os.PathLike):
344	                        content_list.append({"type": "image", "image": os.fspath(image)})
345	                    else:
346	                        raise TypeError(
347	                            f"image must be dict, PIL.Image, or path-like, unsupported image type: {type(image)}"
348	                        )
349	                    image_offset += 1
350	                elif segment == "<video>":
351	                    assert video_offset < len(videos), f"video_offset {video_offset} >= len(videos) {len(videos)}"
352	                    video = videos[video_offset]
353	                    if isinstance(video, dict):
354	                        content_list.append({"type": "video", **video})
355	                    elif isinstance(video, str | os.PathLike):
356	                        content_list.append({"type": "video", "video": os.fspath(video)})
357	                    elif isinstance(video, list):
358	                        video = [os.fspath(frame) if isinstance(frame, os.PathLike) else frame for frame in video]
359	                        content_list.append({"type": "video", "video": video})
360	                    else:
361	                        raise TypeError(
362	                            f"video must be dict, list, or path-like, unsupported video type: {type(video)}"
363	                        )
364	                    video_offset += 1
365	                elif segment == "<audio>":
366	                    assert audio_offset < len(audios), f"audio_offset {audio_offset} >= len(audios) {len(audios)}"
367	                    audio = audios[audio_offset]
368	                    if isinstance(audio, dict):
369	                        payload = dict(audio)
370	                        payload["type"] = "audio"
371	                        if "audio" not in payload and "audio_url" not in payload:
372	                            payload = {"type": "audio", "audio": audio}
373	                        content_list.append(payload)
374	                    else:
375	                        content_list.append({"type": "audio", "audio": audio})
376	                    audio_offset += 1
377	                else:
378	                    content_list.append({"type": "text", "text": segment})
379	            message["content"] = content_list
380	
381	        assert image_offset == len(images), f"image_offset {image_offset} != len(images) {len(images)}"
382	        assert video_offset == len(videos), f"video_offset {video_offset} != len(videos) {len(videos)}"
383	        assert audio_offset == len(audios), f"audio_offset {audio_offset} != len(audios) {len(audios)}"
384	        return messages

413	    @classmethod
414	    async def process_vision_info(
415	        cls,
416	        messages: list[dict],
417	        image_patch_size,
418	        config: DictConfig,
419	    ) -> tuple[list[Image.Image], list[tuple[torch.Tensor, dict]]]:
420	        """Extract images and videos from messages.
421	
422	        This method is called by AgentLoop (e.g SingleTurnAgentLoop) before apply_chat_template to
423	        the `raw_prompt` from dataset. User may customize RLHFDataset and override this method to
424	        support custom vision extraction.
425	
426	        >>> messages = kwargs["raw_prompt"]
427	        >>> images, videos = RLHFDataset.process_vision_info(messages, image_patch_size)
428	        >>> videos, video_metadatas = zip(*videos)
429	        >>> raw_prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)
430	        >>> inputs = processor(text=[raw_prompt], images=images, videos=videos,
431	        ...                    video_metadata=video_metadatas, do_sample_frames=False)
432	
433	        Args:
434	            messages: List of messages from dataset `raw_prompt`.
435	            image_patch_size: Image patch size for processor.
436	            config: Config for dataset.
437	
438	        Returns:
439	            images: List of images.
440	            videos: List of videos, each video is a tuple of (video_tensor, video_metadata).
441	        """
442	        from qwen_vl_utils import process_vision_info
443	
444	        # When called from an AgentLoop, many trajectory coroutines share one
445	        # event loop. ``process_vision_info`` does synchronous PNG decode +
446	        # smart_resize (CPU-heavy); running it inline blocks the loop and starves
447	        # every sibling coroutine's socket I/O (manifests as connect timeouts /
448	        # zero-window stalls under concurrency). Offload to a thread: PIL/numpy
449	        # release the GIL during decode/resize, so the loop stays responsive and
450	        # the work parallelizes across threads. This method is ``async`` and only
451	        # ever awaited from an AgentLoop (which always has a running loop), so
452	        # ``get_running_loop()`` is safe here.
453	        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
454	        images, videos = await loop.run_in_executor(
455	            None,
456	            lambda: process_vision_info(messages, image_patch_size=image_patch_size, return_video_metadata=True),
457	        )
458	        return images, videos

460	    @classmethod
461	    def _extract_audio_info(cls, messages: list[dict]) -> list[Any]:
462	        audios = []
463	        for message in messages:
464	            content = message.get("content")
465	            if not isinstance(content, list):
466	                continue
467	            for item in content:
468	                if not isinstance(item, dict) or item.get("type") != "audio":
469	                    continue
470	                if "audio" in item:
471	                    audios.append(item["audio"])
472	                elif "audio_url" in item:
473	                    audios.append(item["audio_url"])
474	                else:
475	                    audios.append({k: v for k, v in item.items() if k != "type"})
476	        return audios or None

510	    def split(self, num_splits: int):
511	        """
512	        split the dataset into num_splits sub-datasets
513	        Args:
514	            num_splits: specified number of splits
515	        Returns:
516	            List[RLHFDataset]: list of RLHFDataset splits
517	        Raises:
518	            ValueError: if num_splits is not a positive integer
519	        """
520	        if not isinstance(num_splits, int) or num_splits <= 0:
521	            raise ValueError(f"num_splits must be a positive integer, got {num_splits}")
522	
523	        if not hasattr(self, "dataframe"):
524	            raise AttributeError(
525	                "dataframe not found in RLHFDataset\n"
526	                "reason: _read_files_and_tokenize() not called or Parquet file loading failed"
527	            )
528	        if self.dataframe is None:
529	            raise ValueError("RLHFDataset dataframe 为 None!")
530	
531	        total_samples = len(self.dataframe)
532	        print(f"total_samples: {total_samples}")
533	        if total_samples == 0:
534	            raise ValueError("Cannot split an empty dataset")
535	
536	        # Calculate effective sample count after dropping remainders if needed
537	        if total_samples % num_splits != 0:
538	            total_samples = total_samples - (total_samples % num_splits)
539	            logging.warning(f"Dropping {len(self.dataframe) % num_splits} samples, effective samples: {total_samples}")
540	
541	        split_size = total_samples // num_splits
542	        splits = []
543	
544	        for i in range(num_splits):
545	            start_idx = i * split_size
546	            end_idx = (i + 1) * split_size if i < num_splits - 1 else total_samples
547	
548	            split_dataframe = self.dataframe.select(range(start_idx, end_idx))
549	
550	            split_dataset = RLHFDataset(
551	                data_files=self.data_files,
552	                tokenizer=self.tokenizer,
553	                config=self.config,
554	                processor=self.processor,
555	                max_samples=self.max_samples,
556	            )
557	            split_dataset.dataframe = split_dataframe
558	            split_dataset.serialize_dataset = self.serialize_dataset
559	            split_dataset.original_data_files = self.original_data_files
560	
561	            splits.append(split_dataset)
562	
563	        return splits

My earlier repr truncation at 300 chars was misleading — the full outputs DO contain "#### 55 hours old". So the reward is fine: at step 1, 24 responses had #### but all scored 0 (wrong answers); at step 100, 853 have #### and 596 score 1. So learning DID happen (format learned, accuracy 48-58%).

So rewards: 0.0 → 0.55-0.6, then plateau. Accuracy plateau ~0.48-0.58. That's plausible learning for GSM8K on Qwen2.5-0.5B (its pass@1 ~35-45% base, RL can push to ~50-60%).

One puzzle: entropy *rises* (2.86) while samples *collapse* toward identical. There's a clean hypothesis that resolves it: **when π_top ≥ 0.5, the top_p=0.5 nucleus is a single token — sampling degenerates to greedy**. Identical groups should then be the sharp/templated ones. Let me test that prediction:
steps.reasoning_content:
Diversity collapse confirmed: mean unique responses per group falls from 7.60 (step 1) to 3.52 (step 100); 45/128 groups fully identical at step 100; 109/128 zero-variance (all-same score → GRPO advantage exactly 0 for the entire group).

This is the classic GRPO exploration-collapse pathology caused by truncated-tail sampling: top_p=0.5 prunes the sampling support every step. As the policy sharpens toward the top-p mass, responses within a group become increasingly identical, zeroing advantages on ~85% of groups, so the effective gradient signal shrinks, and — importantly — the surviving signal (and the clipped-region fraction) becomes dominated by the small number of groups with reward contrast, producing the unstable entropy trajectory. Note the entropy actually *increases* in the frozen run (0.26 → 2.86) — a sign that the KL term and the PPO objective on the reduced-support distribution are misbehaving.

But wait — is entropy *increase* consistent with diversity *collapse*? The policy's entropy (as measured by actor/entropy over its own samples) goes UP while sample diversity goes DOWN. These seem contradictory, but they are actually both explainable if the sampled tokens come from a renormalized head-and-shoulders distribution: the *recorded* entropy from the actor's full softmax on those tokens could be higher... hmm.

Actually let me think about the mechanics carefully, because the report needs a defensible causal chain:

1. vLLM with top_p=0.5 samples tokens from the renormalized nucleus: π_topk ∝ π·1[π in top-0.5 mass]/Z.
2. The actor (training engine) computes old_log_prob and the PPO ratio with the FULL softmax π_θ.
3. Ratio r = π_θ_new/π_θ_old with π_old = full-softmax probs. On-policy, at step start, r=1. So the importance-ratio mechanics are unbiased w.r.t. the full-softmax policy — standard practice. GRPO with top_p sampling is used widely (many papers sample with temperature/top_p and treat π_old as the full softmax; the induced stationary distribution is the truncated one, which effectively *is* the policy being optimized; this is standard and usually fine).
4. The pathology: with top_p=0.5 and a 0.5B model, the sampled support is small (often just 1-5 tokens per position). The gradients only flow through sampled tokens; tokens outside the nucleus never receive positive gradient mass from sampling but DO receive the entropy/KL regularization through... well, entropy is computed over sampled tokens only.

Why would entropy explode upward? Let me think about the PPO loss with GRPO zero-advantage groups. When the whole group has identical reward (109/128 groups at step 100), advantage = 0 for all tokens → pg_loss contribution 0. Only groups with reward contrast contribute. With group-normalized advantage, a group with 1 correct + 7 wrong gives +1 to the correct and −1/7 to each wrong. The wrong ones are typically long rambling responses; correct ones shorter.

The KL loss (low_var_kl, coef 0.001) anchors to ref model. If pg updates push probability mass around aggressively on a small support, KL grows to 0.39 — that's actually big for coef 0.001. The ref-KL of 0.39 nats/token is substantial drift.

Also clip_ratio 0.18-0.24 at step 100 means 18-24% of response tokens are outside the PPO trust region at update time — the policy is moving more than 20% per batch (e^-0.2 ratio bounds). The control has clip_ratio 0.0088 (0.9%). So the frozen run is taking hugely aggressive updates, which is consistent with a smaller effective gradient batch (only ~19 groups contributing signal out of 128) and possibly larger per-token advantages.

Hmm wait, but with advantage zero on 85% of groups, the gradient is *smaller*, not larger. Why would updates be more aggressive? Because the token-mean loss aggregation: with most tokens having zero advantage, the denominator (mean over response tokens)... token-mean divides by total valid tokens, so zero-advantage tokens don't inflate the denominator... Actually token-mean means loss = sum(pg)/num_tokens; zero-adv tokens contribute zero to numerator. So loss is small. But lr is constant at 2e-6; small gradients → small updates. Yet clip_ratio 0.18 says big updates. Contradiction?

Alternatively, maybe the entropy explosion is driven by the pg loss on positive-advantage tokens... In the frozen run, score/mean reaches 0.55-0.65, meaning among groups with contrast, correct answers get boosted. As correct answers are shorter and have specific format ("#### N"), the model gets reinforced toward a narrow mode... but that would DECREASE entropy, as in control (0.085).

Actually, hmm, let me reconsider: maybe the entropy explosion is a *symptom of numerical/estimation pathology* tied to how the entropy is *measured*. actor/entropy is computed from old_log_prob recompute pass, over response_mask tokens of sampled responses, token-mean aggregated. If the sampled responses are increasingly made of tokens that the full-softmax policy assigns moderate probability (because nucleus sampling concentrates on the head), entropy measured = −E[log π_θ(sample)] should be... For nucleus sampling with Z ≈ 0.5, sampled tokens have π ≥ tail threshold; E[−log π] under nucleus-sampling is bounded by H(nucleus) + log Z... Hold on — maybe I'm overanalyzing the entropy number. The two runs' trajectories: control entropy falls 0.54→0.085; frozen rises 0.26→2.86. In both, the model solves ~50% val.     final_solution = final_solution.split("#### ")[1].replace(",", "")

import json, re, torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

MODEL = "/workspace/models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda")
model.eval()

rows = pq.read_table("/workspace/data/gsm8k/test.parquet").to_pylist()[:32]
pat = re.compile(r"#### (\-?[0-9\.\,]+)")

def gen_ids(ids):
    ids = torch.tensor([ids], device="cuda")
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False,
                             pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tok.eos_token_id)
    return out[0][ids.shape[1]:].tolist()

Q = [r["prompt"][0]["content"] for r in rows]
GT = [r["reward_model"]["ground_truth"] for r in rows]

variants = {}

# A: standard chat template (default system prompt)
variants["A_standard"] = [tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": q}], tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True) for q in Q]

# B: no system prompt - custom minimal ChatML
def chatml_user_only(q):
    return tok("<|im_start|>user\n" + q + "<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n", add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
variants["B_nosystem"] = [chatml_user_only(q) for q in Q]

# C: plain text with role words, NO ChatML markers (double-decode artifact)
def plain(q):
    full = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": q}], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    return tok(full, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
variants["C_full_retokenized"] = [plain(q) for q in Q]

# D: raw user text, no template
variants["D_raw"] = [tok(q, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] for q in Q]

for name, prompts in variants.items():
    n_hash = n_strict = n_boxed = n_latex = n_correct = 0
    lens = []
    for ids, gt in zip(prompts, GT):
        resp_ids = gen_ids(ids)
        resp = tok.decode(resp_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
        lens.append(len(resp_ids))
        m = pat.findall(resp)
        if "####" in resp: n_hash += 1
        if m:
            n_strict += 1
            if m[-1].replace(",", "").replace("$", "") == str(gt): n_correct += 1
        if "\\boxed" in resp: n_boxed += 1
        if "\\(" in resp or "\\[" in resp or "\\boxed" in resp: n_latex += 1
    lens.sort()
    print(f"{name:22s} N={len(prompts)} any####={n_hash} strict={n_strict} correct={n_correct} boxed={n_boxed} latex={n_latex} medlen={lens[len(lens)//2]} maxlen={lens[-1]} capped={sum(1 for l in lens if l>=512)}")

This is peculiar. Normally entropy regularization is off (entropy_coeff=0). In vanilla PPO/GRPO, entropy of the actor's distribution on ITS OWN sampled responses should stay moderate. A rise to 3-4 nats/token with maintained ~0.55 reward is actually the signature of... hmm.

Wait — actually, there's a well-known scenario: the "actor/entropy" metric is computed during _compute_old_log_prob on the responses generated by the rollout engine (vLLM), i.e., entropy of the FSDP actor policy on vLLM-generated tokens. If the actor weights get corrupted/overshot relative to the rollout engine (update_weights not syncing), entropy on rollout samples could blow up. But update_weights is called every step (timing_s/update_weights?). steps.message: A decisive experiment: validation runs greedy (do_sample=False). If the actor weights themselves are degraded, val outputs will show garbage too; if val outputs are clean while rollout outputs are garbage, the problem is in the rollout sampling path, not the actor.
steps.reasoning_content:
Wait — CRITICAL observation here!

`batch_num_tokens = data["loss_mask"].sum()` — this is computed in `forward_backward_batch` on the MINI-BATCH data (256 rows). The loss for each micro-batch is `masked_sum / batch_num_tokens * dp_size` where batch_num_tokens is the mini-batch's total tokens. So the SUM of micro losses = mini-batch mean loss. backward each → accumulated gradient = gradient of mini-batch mean loss. Then optimizer_step once per mini-batch. Correct.

BUT WAIT — where is `global_batch_size` injected into data for ppo_loss? ppo_loss reads data["global_batch_size"] — but here forward_backward_batch only assigns sp_size, batch_num_tokens, dp_size. global_batch_size was assigned in _update_actor (tu.assign_non_tensor(batch_td, global_batch_size=ppo_mini_batch_size...)) — on the FULL batch. Then make_iterator selects rows for the mini-batch — does index_select_tensor_dict propagate non-tensor scalars? The mini_batch_td would carry global_batch_size=256 (a global scalar, still 256 as set). Hmm, but _update_actor sets global_batch_size=ppo_mini_batch_size=256 AND mini_batch_size=256. In train_mini_batch, mini_batch_size=256 popped. global_batch_size remains 256 in each mini_batch. ppo_loss uses global_batch_size only for seq-mean modes and for the metric_aggregation decision (SUM). Fine.

So token-mean: each micro loss = masked_sum_micro / batch_num_tokens_minibatch × dp_size(=1). Accumulated = mean over minibatch response tokens. AdamW step. Standard. 4 optimizer steps per training step.

So the update path is fully standard. Everything checks out. Hmm.

Wait — hold on. Let me look at line 643 again: `batch_num_tokens = data["loss_mask"].sum()`. `loss_mask` comes from left_right_2_no_padding: data["loss_mask"] = data["response_mask"]. For the MINI-batch of 256 rows (nested jagged), sum = total response tokens in mini-batch ~256×280 ≈ 71k. pg_loss per micro = masked_sum(pg_loss_micro)/71k × 1. Wait, but masked_sum is over the MICRO batch (subset). Sum over micros = 71k-token sum / 71k = mean. ✓.

Alright — so the update loop is airtight standard.

Hmm, so now let me look at THE one remaining piece I haven't verified in the update chain: the fsdp `forward_step` for the TRAINING path — for the loss computation path (logits → log_probs of response tokens, the roll/shift for TRAINING, response_mask alignment in NO_PADDING mode). We read the INFER path prepare_model_outputs (rmpad, lines 1120-1341) but the TRAINING forward_step (with loss_function) is elsewhere (line ~1360 per summary). Let me read it. The training forward_step computes log_probs via logits_processor / logprobs_from_logits with rolled labels and calls loss_function. The key subtlety: for the TRAIN path, log_probs are also computed with the same roll; then in ppo_loss, log_prob = no_padding_2_padding(model_output["log_probs"], data) — the same alignment as old_log_probs. Since ppo_kl (log_prob vs old_log_prob) is tiny and consistent, both paths agree — meaning training and old_log_prob paths produce the same values (both correct or both identically wrong — but they're the same code, so consistency is guaranteed).

The real question: is the alignment of log_probs vs response_mask correct? If BOTH old_log_prob and training log_prob are shifted the same way, then ratio is correct, and the gradient pushes π toward higher advantage responses... but with a WRONG alignment, e.g., log_prob of response token i actually being log π(x_{i+1}) paired with advantage of token i (outcome advantage broadcast — SAME for all tokens of the response!). For OUTCOME reward (GRPO), the advantage is IDENTICAL for every response token. So a ONE-TOKEN SHIFT in log-prob alignment does NOT change the gradient direction (each token's gradient weight is the same A)! It only changes... nothing at all for outcome rewards, since A is constant across the response.

BUT the KL loss (vs ref_log_prob, per-token) — a shift would corrupt the KL: comparing log π(x_{i+1}) with ref log π(x_i) — that would create a systematic positive KL bias → kl_loss growing... AND, crucially, a misaligned KL would push the policy in a WRONG direction (trying to match ref's log-probs at wrong positions — an unachievable target → drift/garbage!). Interesting!! And kl_loss metric: growing from 0.0001 (step 2, actor≈ref so misalignment produces... wait, at step 2 actor==ref almost, so misaligned KL comparison would NOT be ~0. It would be E[kl(x_{i+1} vs x_i)] > 0 immediately. Observed kl_loss at step 2 = 0.000139 — near zero. At step 2 the actor had one tiny update (grad_norm 0.07 at step... wait step 1 grad 0). If old/ref/log alignment were shifted, kl_loss at step 2 would already be substantial (cross-position KL ~ 1-5 nats). It's 0.000139 — so alignment is CORRECT.

OK so KL alignment correct. Everything in the actor update is verified correct. Hmm.

So — if the actor update is correct and the reward is correct and GRPO grouping is correct, then the observed entropy explosion must come from the DATA the update sees: i.e., the ROLLOUT. What if the rollout engine samples responses with a DIFFERENT policy than the actor? E.g., weights synced wrongly (partial/stale), or the rollout engine's sampling params (temperature 1.0 top_p 0.5) but the TRAINING-side recompute uses temperature from meta_info...

Hmm wait, actually — think about this scenario: the rollout engine samples at temperature 1.0, and the FSDP actor computes log probs dividing logits by temperature=1.0. Fine.

But WAIT — what about the response_token_ids actually TRAINED on? What if the rollout returns responses that are MISALIGNED with the prompts (e.g., responses attached to the wrong prompts after the n-sampling or after async manager gathering)? Then: reward computed on (prompt, response) pairs — the GSM8K rule checks the response's #### N vs the prompt's gold answer — misaligned pairs would score ~0 mostly... but scores are 0.53. Hmm, no.

What if responses were fine but the loss saw DIFFERENT responses (e.g., a repeat/union mismatch)? Then log_prob/old_log_prob would be computed on the true responses (both same), so no.

Hmm, what about PROMPT truncation — max_prompt_length 512, filter_overlong_prompts=True, truncation=error. Prompts ≤512. Fine.

OK, let me now go look at the actual vLLM rollout code myself (not waiting for the agent) — specifically the parts most likely to carry a planted defect for THIS run: sampling params construction (temperature/top_p), n handling, and the async rollout manager's gather. And crucially `rollout_log_probs` handling. Actually, wait — first, let me look at the entropy metric itself one more time. Is `actor/entropy` possibly just WRONG (computed on garbage alignment) while the model is actually fine? But the gibberish in the dumps is REAL (vLLM generated it) — the model really is degraded. Both agree.

Actually — hmm, wait. Let me re-examine the gibberish claim. "outputs begin as coherent math then degrade into multilingual garbage". 227/1024 outputs with >5% non-ASCII. Let me quantify more: how many of those have the garbage in the LATTER portion? If the model were healthy, top_p=0.5 sampling... a 0.5B model at temp 1.0/top_p 0.5 CAN occasionally wander into multilingual tokens — 22% of outputs having >5% non-ASCII is a lot though.

Hmm, hold on. Let me reconsider the temperature used by vLLM. If the rollout sampled at a HIGHER temperature than 1.0 (e.g., config wiring bug: rollout.temperature read from wrong field, or divided/multiplied somewhere), the SAMPLES would be garbage-y — entropy of the SAMPLES high... but actor/entropy is the actor's OWN entropy at those tokens, computed by FSDP actor at temperature 1.0 (logits/1.0). A healthy actor at temp 1.0 would have entropy 0.26-0.5 even on garbage tokens (entropy is a property of the actor's distribution at those CONTEXTS; garbage context → higher entropy, but 3-4 nats sustained?).

Hmm — actually, that's a real effect: entropy measured ON high-temperature-generated tokens is biased upward because garbage context raises the actor's own entropy. If the rollout engine sampled at, say, temperature 2.0 (misconfigured), then: samples would be noisy/gibberish (227/1024 with non-ASCII garbage!), rewards would still be ~0.5 (some correct), and the actor's entropy MEASURED ON those samples would be elevated (entropy at garbage contexts is high). But would it reach 3-4 nats mean over all tokens? If 22% of outputs are garbage with entropy ~6-8 and 78% healthy with ~0.5-1, mean ≈ 0.22×7 + 0.78×0.8 ≈ 2.1. To hit 3.2 you'd need more.

But ALSO: training on high-temperature samples with GRPO — the policy gradient pushes up probability of rewarded samples (correct answers, which at temp 2.0 are rarer but exist) — the model would still learn. Entropy drift upward — the on-policy distribution mismatch (π sampled at T≠1 while π trained at T=1... wait, the training log probs are at temperature 1.0 — the "policy" being optimized is the T=1 distribution, but samples come from the T=2 distribution — importance mismatch! The ratio exp(log π_T1 − old_log_prob_T1) — both at T=1 — so PPO doesn't see the mismatch! The samples come from a DIFFERENT (higher-entropy) distribution than the anchor. Training on off-policy-ish samples: PPO ratio starts at 1 (both recomputed at T=1)... so the update doesn't "know" the samples came from a flattened distribution. GRPO would push up the T=1 probability of the correct answers (good) and push down wrong ones — but the wrong ones at T=2 include lots of high-entropy garbage; pushing down garbage tokens is fine...

Hmm, would the actor itself become high-entropy (its own T=1 entropy 3-4)? The PPO objective with correct ratio anchoring should NOT inflate the actor's entropy... unless the off-policy mismatch effectively adds noise.

Hmm, wait. Actually, I realize I should simply check the val dumps! Validation runs with do_sample=False (greedy) and val_kwargs.n=1. val_generations/50.jsonl and 100.jsonl exist. If the ACTOR is truly degraded (high entropy), greedy decoding would still produce coherent output (greedy = argmax, robust to entropy inflation as long as the argmax is right). Val acc at 50 = 0.46, at 100 = 0.49 — reasonable. But let me look at the actual val outputs at step 50/100 for signs of degradation (garbage after ####, weird tokens). If val outputs are CLEAN and the rollout outputs are garbage, that suggests the ROLLOUT sampling is the problem (temperature/sampler), not the actor weights. If val outputs also show garbage, the actor weights themselves are degraded.

That's a decisive experiment. Let me look at val_generations/50.jsonl and 100.jsonl content.

UNLESS the entropy computation and NLL are computed on different token subsets or the batch for old_log_prob isn't the same as the rollout batch... OR the NLL is inflated by a subset of tokens with near-zero prob (per-token bimodality) while entropy is an average including many low-entropy tokens.

On-policy identity: E_{x~q}[−ln π(x)] = H(π) + KL(q||π) ≥ H(π) when q=π. With top_p sampling, q ≠ π: q has support only on the nucleus. KL(q||π) = E_q[ln q − ln π]. E_q[ln q] = −H(q) where H(q) = nucleus entropy + ln... hmm wait, if vLLM samples from renormalized nucleus and records logprobs ln q = ln π_topk − ln Z where Z = sum of nucleus probs ≈ 0.5+. Then −E_q[ln q] = H(q) + ln... no: E_q[−ln q] = H(q) exactly (that's the definition of cross-entropy of q with itself = entropy). E_q[−ln π] = H(q) + KL(q||π) where KL(q||π) = E_q[ln(q/π)] = E_q[−ln Z] = ln(1/Z) ≈ ln 2 = 0.69 max (Z ≥ 0.5 when nucleus cut at 0.5 cumulative... Z = sum of kept probs ≥ 0.5 by construction, ≤ 1; so KL ≤ ln2 ≈ 0.69).

So E_q[−ln π] ≤ H(q) + 0.69. If measured mean NLL were 1.41 nats/token, then H(q) ≥ 0.72. Fine. And actor entropy (measured as H(π) per-token on the batch positions) = 2.86 — H(π) should be ≥ H(q) + KL... no, relation between H(π) and H(q): q is π truncated+renormalized to the nucleus. H(q) vs H(π): H(q) = −Σ_nucleus q_i ln q_i. For a sharp π (one token at 0.9, rest spread), H(π) could be low... but truncation REMOVES tail mass, which can RAISE or LOWER entropy depending. Hmm, this is getting deep. The empirical facts: actor entropy 2.86 (per-token, presumably averaged over response positions of the whole batch), training_log_ppl... 

I need to be careful about what training_log_ppl is: from my earlier reading of rollout_corr_helper.compute_offpolicy_metrics: `training_ppl = torch.exp(-masked_mean(old_log_prob, response_mask, axis=-1)).mean()`. masked_mean with axis=-1 gives PER-SEQUENCE mean logprob; then exp(−mean) per sequence; then .mean() over sequences. So training_ppl=945.6 = mean_seq exp(−mean_logprob_seq). And training_log_ppl=1.4098: is that the mean over sequences of mean_logprob? From summary: "log_ppl_diff = mean_log_prob_rollout − mean_log_prob_training, ppl_ratio". And training_log_ppl is presumably masked_mean over everything = mean per-token logprob... If training_log_ppl = 1.41 as a POSITIVE number, it's likely reported as −mean_logprob i.e. NLL. So average per-token NLL ≈ 1.41 nats. Hmm, but then exp(mean) would be ~4, while mean of exps is 945 → massive per-sequence variance: some sequences with NLL ~7+.

Actor entropy 2.86 vs mean NLL 1.41: violates H(π) ≤ E_q[−ln π] identity... UNLESS entropy is computed per-token including... hmm, actually wait — is actor/entropy the entropy of the FULL next-token distribution at each position (H(π(·|prefix))) averaged over positions? Yes: computed in compute_log_prob via entropy of logits. And E_q[−ln π(x)] over sampled x at those positions = H(q) + KL(q||π). On-policy with top_p=1, q=π, equality H(π) = NLL. With top_p=0.5, NLL = H(q) + KL(q||π) ≤ H(q) + ln 2.

So NLL(1.41) < H(π)(2.86) requires H(q) + KL < H(π), i.e., H(q) < H(π) − KL: the RENORMALIZED NUCLEUS DISTRIBUTION has LOWER entropy than the full distribution?? Impossible in general? Entropy of renormalized truncation: H(q) = −Σ_{i∈N} q_i ln q_i. Consider π = (0.5, 0.5×spread over 1000 tokens). Nucleus (top_p=0.5) could be just {token1} if its mass ≥0.5... then q = δ, H(q)=0. H(π) large. So yes, H(q) ≪ H(π) is possible! And NLL = H(q)+KL ≈ 0 + ln(1/Z) = ln 2 ≈ 0.69 on those sharp positions.

So on SHARP positions: NLL ≈ ln2 ≈ 0.69, entropy H(π) can be anything (large if the tail is spread). On FLAT positions (nucleus = many tokens): H(q) ≈ H(π) truncated...

Averaged: NLL 1.41, H(π) 2.86. Consistent if many positions are sharp-with-fat-tails (H(π) high, NLL low) — e.g., a 0.5B model that puts 0.55 on the greedy token and spreads 0.45 over a long flat tail → H(π) ≈ 0.55·0.6 + tail entropy ~ 2-4 nats; NLL ≈ 0.69 (all sampled tokens are the top token or nucleus few). And the high-ppl sequences (NLL~7): those are positions where the SAMPLED token had prob e^-7 under π — happens when nucleus isn't tiny... wait if nucleus includes the sampled token, its π-prob ≥ ... nucleus at cumulative 0.5 — the sampled token is IN the nucleus so π(x) ≥ (smallest nucleus member) — could still be small if nucleus is many flat tokens: π(x) ≈ 0.5/K for K tokens → ln π ≈ −ln(2K); for K=1000, ln π ≈ −7.3! There it is: the long all-unique rambling responses correspond to positions where the model is FLAT over ~1000 tokens (uncertain continuation mid-derivation), samples a token with π ≈ 1/2000, NLL ≈ 7.6. These flat positions also have H(π) ≈ ln(1000)+... ≈ 7 nats. Hmm, but average entropy is 2.86.

OK — the quantitative paradox resolves as mixture: (sharp positions: H(π) moderate-to-high due to flat tails, NLL≈0.7) + (flat positions: H(π) high ≈ 7, NLL ≈ 7). The average H(π)=2.86 is BELOW the per-position NLL average... no, NLL average is 1.41 < 2.86. For the mixture: NLL_avg = Σ_i w_i (H_i(q) + KL_i). Sharp: 0.69ish; flat: ~7. To average 1.41 with, say, 10% flat positions at 7 → 0.7+0.7=1.4 ✓. And H(π) average = sharp positions contribute H_π (could be 2-3 each due to flat tails over 1000+ tokens) — 0.9×2.5 + 0.1×7 ≈ 2.95 ✓. Consistent!

But WHY does the frozen run develop flat-tailed sharp-headed distributions where the control doesn't? THIS is the actual training-dynamics consequence of top_p=0.5 sampling: the sampled tokens are ALWAYS nucleus members (the top token whenever π_top ≥ 0.5). GRPO reinforces (positive advantage) or suppresses (negative advantage) the SAMPLED tokens only. With all-correct groups (greedy-collapse) getting advantage 0 (no signal) and the signal coming from contrast groups... the policy gradient pushes up logprob of tokens in correct responses. Tokens NOT sampled in the tail never get directly reinforced — but they're part of the softmax normalization: pushing up sampled-token logits pushes down... no, softmax: increasing logit of sampled tokens decreases prob of all others proportionally. But actually the entropy EXPLODES — meaning logits get flatter over training on some positions. Hmm, how? If we only ever increase sampled-token logits, entropy should DECREASE (sharpen) as in the control (0.54 → 0.085).

Wait — control entropy goes DOWN to 0.085 (super sharp). Frozen entropy goes UP to 2.86-3.2. What increases entropy? Negative advantage on sampled tokens (wrong answers get suppressed → their logits pushed down → alternative tokens' probs rise → flattening). In GRPO with group-normalized advantages: within a contrast group, correct responses get +, wrong get −. The wrong-but-sampled tokens get suppressed. With top_p=0.5, WHICH tokens get sampled? Disproportionately the argmax tokens on sharp positions; suppression of argmax tokens flattens the distribution (raises entropy) — and the flattened distribution makes the nucleus WIDER next step (more diversity in the wrong directions), which samples low-prob tokens... runaway entropy. Meanwhile the control samples the full support: wrong responses sample a representative mix; suppression acts on a REPRESENTATIVE set of tokens; the net effect sharpens onto the correct modes.

Also the training_ppl explosion (945) is consistent: after the policy flattens, the batch contains long flat-position continuations where the sampled token has tiny π (KL of renormalized nucleus etc.). Actually more precisely — training_ppl measures exp(−mean logprob) per sequence — sequences with many flat positions (nucleus-sample at ~e^-7) blow up. So the "ppl explosion" is a symptom of the entropy blowup + tail-sampling, NOT a weightsync failure (pearson 0.986 confirms engines agree).

There's ALSO the subtle bias: importance ratio r = π_θ(x)/π_old(x) where π_old is the ACTOR's own recomputed logprob of sampled tokens — unbiased wrt the true π at sampling time (since vLLM's renormalization only changes WHICH tokens get sampled, not the correctness of old_log_prob values). So the training math is CORRECT; the pathology is purely EXPLORATION/distribution: which tokens enter the gradient. Under top_p=0.5 with sharpening policy, groups collapse to greedy duplicates (zero advantage) and the remaining signal comes from suppressing majority-token continuations in wrong groups → entropy blowup + ppl blowup + stalling val acc (0.49 vs 0.5565) and stall in training score plateau ~0.55-0.58 (control reaches 0.664).

I'm now quite confident in the mechanism story, and it matches all observed signals:
1. Step-1 probs_diff 0.065/pearson 0.71 (vs control 0.0043/0.9995) — signature of vLLM renormalized logprob recording under top_p=0.5 (diagnostic red herring but confirms setting active).
2. Group diversity collapse: 7.60 unique/group → 3.52; zero-var groups 128→109; all-identical 0→45 (greedy collapse as policy sharpens past π_top=0.5).
3. Entropy explosion 0.26→2.86-3.2 (vs control 0.54→0.085): negative-advantage suppression falls disproportionately on argmax tokens, flattening the distribution.
4. training_ppl 945 / kl_loss 0.39 plateau: consequence of flat distributions + tail... hmm wait, kl_loss is KL(π_θ || π_ref)? No — use_kl_loss with low_var_kl computes KL between π_θ and ref policy per token. Frozen kl_loss 0.39 vs control 0.15 — frozen drifted 2.5x further from ref. Consistent with stronger drift.

Hmm, one more consideration: is kl_loss computed against ref policy (frozen initial model)? Yes (ref_log_prob computed by reference worker). So the frozen run drifted much further from the initial policy than control — despite SAME KL coef — because the advantage signal kept pushing (the entropy feedback loop) whereas control converged.

5. Response clip_ratio 0.18-0.24 vs control 0.009-0.03: fraction of responses hitting 512-token cap. Flat/rambling policy → more truncated responses. The overlong penalty is DISABLED (overlong_buffer_cfg.enable=False), so truncated rambling responses that happen to contain a correct #### still get score 1 — rewarding degenerate rambling. But control also has it disabled... it's the same config, so not THE defect, but it amplifies the frozen pathology.

All consistent: single root cause top_p=0.5.

Also, one alternative hypothesis I should explicitly kill: "the defect is the entropy explosion caused by some code bug in entropy computation or the actor update". The config diff proves the ONLY config difference is top_p, and the control ran with the SAME verl code (the control's workspace was /user/user1/pr27-calib/topp-control/workspace — a DIFFERENT copy of the workspace, possibly with different code!). Hmm — wait. Is the control's code identical to the staged code? If the control workspace had a code fix AND top_p=1.0, then my conclusion "only top_p differs" would be about CONFIG, not CODE. The config dump comparison covers the config, not the verl source code. The control ran from a different directory tree. If the graders planted BOTH a code defect and top_p... but no: the frozen run's pathology must be explained by the STAGED code + STAGED config. The control proves: same config-with-top_p=1.0 (on ITS code) is healthy. If the control's code differs from staged code, top_p=1.0 might not fix the staged run.

How can I check whether the control's verl code == staged verl code? The control workspace is OUTSIDE the staged workspace (/user/user1/pr27-calib/topp-control/...) — I decided earlier not to read it (material outside the staged workspace). But comparing file hashes to verify code identity is... reading it. The instruction: "Do not fetch code, documentation, packages, or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose and repair using only what is staged locally." That's about FETCHING from outside (network) primarily, but "or any other material from outside the staged workspace" is broad. My earlier judgment call (in summary): use /tmp/ray runtime logs as health-baseline evidence but do NOT read the control workspace. Hashing files of the control workspace would violate that. I'll stick to that.

Alternative approach to rule out a code-level defect WITHOUT the control workspace: the four audit agents are auditing the staged code paths (actor update, rollout, trainer, data/reward). Their job is exactly this: find any code-level bug. Their verdict "no code defect found in these paths" + my mechanistic account (which explains every metric anomaly via top_p=0.5 sampling dynamics, with no code defect required) + the config-diff evidence gives a complete case.

Also the .pyc evidence: 23 pyc files match source mtime/size — no post-compile source edits. If the graders had planted a code defect in a training-path module, it would be in the source .py (visible to my audits). The audits cover the main paths.

One more direct check I can do myself quickly: diff the staged verl against any pristine copy staged locally... is there one? E.g., a verl wheel/tarball in the workspace? Let me check if there's a site-packages copy or a backup. Earlier established: "no site-packages verl". So no local pristine copy. The audits are the way.

While waiting for the agents, let me also double-check the claim "val_kwargs top_p=1.0" — from the config diff, val_kwargs keys matched control (n=1, do_sample=False/temp 0, top_p=1.0 both) — validation is greedy in both, so held-out eval is unaffected by the top_p defect; the damage is purely through training dynamics. Good — that's why val acc still reaches 0.49 in the frozen run (learning happens, just worse).

Also confirm the frozen val acc numbers from run100/val_generations vs my re-score (0.4860@100) — done pre-compaction, matches.

Now, expected effect of fix: rerun with top_p=1.0 should reproduce the control's health: step-100 val acc ~0.55 (vs 0.486), entropy declining to ~0.1-0.3 (vs exploding to 2.86), training_ppl ~1.1 (vs 945), kl_loss ~0.15 (vs 0.39), response clip_ratio ~1-3% (vs 18-24%), score/mean reaching ~0.66 (vs 0.58), group diversity maintained (≥7 unique/group).

Wait — one important nuance: the control ran with a DIFFERENT data path (/user/.../topp-control/workspace/data/...)? The control config showed data.train_files=/user/user1/pr27-calib/topp-control/workspace/data/gsm8k/train.parquet — the control used ITS OWN copy of the data. If the control's data differed from staged data... the parquet is sha-pinned at grading (staged data is the ground truth). The control's data copy is presumably identical (the calibration infra copies the workspace). I can't verify without reading outside. Fine — the audit agents verified the staged data is clean (pinned, correct prompts, correct gold answers).

Let me now wait for/collect the agent results. Check ListAgents again — they were started 19+ min ago as of the last check (several minutes back). Let me look at their partial outputs to gauge progress (the system-reminder says I can read partial output files). Since these are audit agents whose conclusions I need, and they may be near done, I'll peek at the tail of each output file... the reminder said don't cat directly (full transcripts), but reading the tail portion is fine to gauge. steps.message:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:

The user (parent agent) requested a read-only audit of a staged verl (RL post-training framework) checkout at `/workspace` to find a PLANTED DEFECT in the ROLLOUT/GENERATION path. Context: a GSM8K GRPO run (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, FSDP + vLLM, 1 GPU) launched with: `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name=vllm`, `rollout.tensor_model_parallel_size=1`, `rollout.gpu_memory_utilization=0.4`, `rollout.n=8`, `rollout.temperature=1.0`, `rollout.top_p=0.5`, `rollout.top_k=-1`, `rollout.seed=42`, `rollout.agent.num_workers=1`, `rollout.val_kwargs.n=1`, `rollout.val_kwargs.do_sample=False`, `data.max_prompt_length=512`, `data.max_response_length=512`, `trainer.use_v1=False`.

Observed frozen-run symptoms (100-step run): ~4-30% of training responses hit the 512-token cap (response_length/clip_ratio up to 0.30); 11-17% of responses contain no "####" at all; ~1 response in 20 in held-out validation is degenerate repetition (e.g., a line of hundreds of zeros); response mean length ~250-340 tokens; entropy of the policy rises steadily (0.26 → 3+ nats).

Required trace: from `verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py` (class RayPPOTrainer, method fit) → generation dispatch (async_rollout_manager / agent loop since `rollout.agent.num_workers=1`) → then read: `/workspace/verl/experimental/agent_loop/agent_loop.py` (+ schemas) — SamplingParams for train vs validation (val_kwargs, do_sample=False handling, temperature/top_p/top_k/seed application, `__do_sample__` flag), response token assembly (stop tokens, EOS handling, truncation at max_response_length), how `rollout_log_probs` is recorded; the vLLM engine wrapper `/workspace/verl/workers/rollout/vllm_rollout/` — sampling params construction, `max_tokens`, stop token ids, `include_stop_str_in_output`, detokenization, logprob recording (post-top_p-renormalized?), seed handling, weight-sync path; rollout config `/workspace/verl/workers/config/rollout.py` and `/workspace/verl/trainer/config/rollout/*.yaml` — default `stop_token_ids`, `max_response_length` wiring, multi_turn/agent settings, TRAIN vs VAL generation differences.

Specific defect hypotheses to check: val generation accidentally sampling (or train/val kwargs swapped), wrong EOS/stop token for Qwen2.5 (eos should be `<|im_end|>`, id 151645; also 151643), stop strings that never match, max_response_length mis-scaled (tokens vs chars), seed pinning that makes all 8 rollouts of a group identical, logprob recording that distorts training (rollout_log_probs used as old_log_probs), missing EOS trimming, detokenization defects.

Required output format: a numbered list of findings, each with file:line, quoted code, why it deviates, and how it connects to the symptoms. If a section is correct, say so briefly. **Do not modify any files.** (Constraints: read-only audit; no file modifications; no report/summary .md files — findings returned directly in the final message; use `python3 -I` when reading untrusted run artifacts; absolute paths only; no emojis.)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - verl RL framework: RayPPOTrainer, FSDP actor, vLLM rollout (async/agent-loop mode), GRPO with group size n=8
   - Agent-loop rollout architecture: AgentLoopManager → AgentLoopWorker (Ray actor) → SingleTurnAgentLoop → LLMServerClient (with aborted-request resume loop) → GlobalRequestLoadBalancer → vLLMHttpServer.generate (token-in/token-out)
   - vLLM 0.17.0 V1 sampling internals: gumbel kernel noise = f(per-request seed, absolute token position); temperature==0 → no noise (pure argmax); top_k/top_p filter logits before noise; per-request seed defaults to a distinct `np.random.randint` draw when SamplingParams.seed is None
   - verl `full_determinism` (false here): gates per-request seed injection (`seed = replica_rank + config.seed`), `det-{priority}` request IDs, `enable_full_determinism`, VERL_FULL_DETERMINISM/VERL_SEED/VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT env vars — all inactive in this run
   - `logprobs_mode: processed_logprobs`: vLLM returns top-1 logprobs computed from PROCESSED (post temperature/top_k/top_p) logits → rollout_log_probs are post-top_p-renormalized (explains rollout_corr ppl_ratio 1.09-1.16); diagnostic-only since `bypass_recomputing_logprofs` is off (timing_s/old_log_prob present in metrics)
   - top_p=0.5 nucleus sampling: when top token probability ≥ top_p, candidate set = single token → sampling forced to argmax regardless of noise → deterministic rollouts on peaked paths
   - Qwen2.5 EOS: `<|im_end|>` (151645) and `<|endoftext|>` (151643) from HF generation_config; tokenizer eos_token '<|im_end|>', pad '<|endoftext|>'; verl sends no explicit stop_token_ids (relies on vLLM EOS handling); HF generation_config repetition_penalty=1.1 neutralized by verl (override_generation_config repetition_penalty=1.0 + per-request `setdefault("repetition_penalty", 1.0)`)
   - GRPO group advantage with n=8; identical rollouts within a group → zero advantage variance → no learning signal for that group
   - Weight sync: checkpoint_manager.update_weights → update_weights_from_ipc → wake_up + reset_prefix_cache (correct)
   - Rollout artifact layout: rollouts/*.jsonl rows are SHUFFLED (128 distinct inputs × 8 each, scattered positions) — must group by identical input, not by consecutive-8/stride-128

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - `/workspace/run_gsm8k_grpo.sh` (read pre-compaction; the run config): TRAIN_BATCH_SIZE=128, ROLLOUT_N=8, PPO_MINI_BATCH_SIZE=32, MAX_PROMPT/RESPONSE_LENGTH=512, ACTOR_LR=2e-6, KL_LOSS_COEF=0.001 (kl_loss_type=low_var_kl), ROLLOUT_TOP_P=0.5, temperature=1.0, top_k=-1, seed=42, TEST_FREQ=10, TOTAL_STEPS=100; entropy_coeff=0, loss_agg_mode=token-mean, use_dynamic_bsz=True; overlong_buffer disabled; trainer.use_v1=False, val_before_train=True; MODEL_PATH=$W/models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. NO full_determinism, NO rollout_correction/bypass settings.

   - `/workspace/verl/trainer/config/rollout/rollout.yaml` (487 lines, re-delivered this session): `full_determinism: false` (27), `seed: 42` (31), `prompt_length/response_length` from data.* (35/39), `ignore_eos: False` (49), `logprobs_mode: processed_logprobs` (93), `do_sample: True` (124), `n: 1` (127), val_kwargs `{top_k: -1, top_p: 1.0, temperature: 0, n: 1, do_sample: False}` (151-170, CORRECT), `calculate_log_probs: True` (233), `agent.num_workers: 8` (run overrides to 1), `default_agent_loop: single_turn_agent` (245), `skip_tokenizer_init: True` (329; note engine args hardcode False), no repetition_penalty key (dataclass default 1.0), no stop_token_ids concept.

   - `/workspace/verl/experimental/agent_loop/single_turn_agent_loop.py` (116 lines, read fully this session):
     ```python
     request_id = f"det-{priority}" if getattr(self.rollout_config, "full_determinism", False) else uuid4().hex   # line 66 → uuid4 per rollout (full_determinism=False)
     ...
     response_ids = output.token_ids
     response_mask = [1] * len(output.token_ids)
     response_logprobs = output.log_probs                                    # lines 91-93
     output: AgentLoopOutput = AgentLoopOutput(
         prompt_ids=prompt_ids,
         response_ids=response_ids[: self.response_length],
         response_mask=response_mask[: self.response_length],
         response_logprobs=response_logprobs[: self.response_length] if response_logprobs else None,   # 95-99: truncation at response_length, no EOS trimming (relies on vLLM)
         ...
         num_turns=2, ...)
     ```
     Correct for this configuration.

   - `/workspace/verl/experimental/agent_loop/agent_loop.py` (regions 100-339, 540-898, 900-1030 read this session; 1-100, 380-540, 1030-1269 still unread):
     - `generate_sequences` (567-659): `sampling_params = dict(temperature=config.temperature, top_p=config.top_p, top_k=config.top_k, repetition_penalty=1.0, logprobs=config.calculate_log_probs)`; validation override `if validate: sampling_params["top_p"]=config.val_kwargs.top_p; ...temperature=config.val_kwargs.temperature`; `apply_greedy_sampling_params` (top_p=1.0, top_k=-1, temperature=0) applied ONLY when `not validate and per_sample_do_sample is not None and not bool(per_sample_do_sample[i])` (REMAX `__do_sample__`, per_sample_do_sample is None here); per-sample `sample_sampling_params = dict(sampling_params)`; one asyncio task per sample.
     - `_pad_token_ids` (696-725): HF tokenizer.pad with max_length, padding_side; pads with tokenizer.pad_token_id (151643 for Qwen).
     - `_agent_loop_postprocess` (727-864): prompt left-pad to prompt_length, response right-pad to response_length; `response_logprobs = torch.tensor(output.response_logprobs + [0.0] * pad_size)` (773-776); `response_mask = response_mask_output["input_ids"] * response_output["attention_mask"]` (778) — verified correct for single-turn (pad positions zeroed by attention_mask); `compute_position_id_with_mask(attention_mask)` for text-only.
     - `AgentLoopOutput.as_dict` (116-147): builds `rollout_log_probs` tensor from response_logprobs; `rm_scores` zeros with reward at last position.

steps.message: The agents are mid-flight. Meanwhile, one more integrity check on my side: whether any staged file was modified *after* the frozen run was produced (11:34) — which would indicate post-run tampering:
steps.reasoning_content:
The agents are still working (output files growing; those are raw transcripts, tails show in-flight API payloads). Their final reports will arrive as task notifications. Meanwhile, let me continue the deep verification myself on the piece that remains most uncertain: the "entropy vs NLL" paradox. 

I want to understand: actor/entropy 2.86 at step 100 but training_log_ppl 1.41 (mean per-token NLL) → e^1.41 = 4.1 ppl... wait no, training_ppl=945 means mean of per-seq PPLs = exp of per-seq mean NLL... 945^(1/... hmm: training_ppl = mean over sequences of exp(mean per-token NLL per sequence). mean log ppl over tokens = training_log_ppl = 1.4098 nats → per-seq typical ppl ~ e^1.41=4.1, but the MEAN of exp is dominated by high-NLL sequences → 945. OK.

So per-token NLL on own samples ≈ 1.41 nats while entropy of the policy (actor/entropy from the same forward pass) = 2.86 nats. For a perfectly on-policy distribution, E[-log π(y)] = H(π) → 1.41 should equal 2.86. A gap of ~1.45 nats is IMPOSSIBLE for on-policy data... UNLESS:

1. The samples were NOT drawn from the distribution whose entropy is measured — i.e., sampling used a DIFFERENT distribution than the actor's softmax. With top_p=0.5, samples come from renormalized nucleus q. E_q[-log π] = H(q) + KL(q||π). The KL between renormalized-nucleus and full distribution can be LARGE when the nucleus is small: if nucleus mass Z=0.6, then log π(y) = log q(y) + log Z + ... roughly E_q[-log π] ≈ H(q) + E_q[-log(π(y)/q(y))]. For tokens where π_top < 0.5 the nucleus includes many tokens (little difference). For tokens where π_top ≥ 0.5, nucleus = {top token} → q = delta → H(q)=0 and -log π(y) = -log π_top which can be small if π_top≈1... hmm that DECREASES NLL, not increases.

Actually the puzzle direction: NLL(1.41) < H(2.86)?? NLL is LOWER than entropy. That means sampled tokens have HIGHER probability under π than the average entropy suggests — i.e., the sampler prefers high-probability tokens more than π would (mode-seeking beyond temperature 1). THAT is exactly what top_p truncation does! Truncation removes the long tail; renormalized nucleus q over-weights the head. E_q[-log π] = H(q) + KL(q||π) ≥ H(q). And H(q) ≤ H(π)... For nucleus sampling: E_q[-log π] = E_q[-log q] + E_q[log q - log π] = H(q) + E_q[log(Z * π(y)/π(y) restricted...)]. Let q(y) = π(y)/Z for y in nucleus S. Then log q - log π = -log Z on S. So E_q[-log π] = H(q) - log Z... wait: -log π(y) = -log(q(y) Z) = -log q(y) - log Z. So E_q[-log π] = H(q) - log Z. Since Z ≥ 0.5, -log Z ≤ log 2 = 0.69. And H(q) = entropy of renormalized nucleus ≤ H(π). So E_q[-log π] ≤ H(π) - log Z. With Z→1 (flat distributions, nucleus=full), gap→0 and NLL≈H. With sharp tokens (Z=π_top), H(q)=0 and NLL = -log π_top = H(π) - (entropy gap)... e.g., π=(0.8, 0.2 split): H=0.5, nucleus={top}, NLL=0.22. So NLL < H is EXPECTED with top_p truncation, bounded below by H - log 2.

Observed: NLL 1.41 vs H 2.86 → gap 1.45 nats >> log 2 = 0.69. Contradiction with pure top_p truncation at the SAME weights!

BUT: entropy (2.86) and NLL (1.41) are computed at DIFFERENT steps/weights. actor/entropy at step N is computed from the actor forward pass on step-N's own rollouts (on-policy at step N: entropy measured on responses generated BY the step-N policy π_N). NLL... wait, old_log_probs also computed in the same forward pass at step N on step N's rollouts. So both same weights, same data. NLL = E[-log π_N(y_N)] where y_N ~ q_N (top_p-0.5 renormalized). H = H(π_N). Gap = H(π_N) - E_qN[-log π_N] = [H(π_N)-H(q_N)] + log Z_N ≤ ... hmm wait I derived E_q[-log π] = H(q) - log Z. So gap = H(π) - H(q) + log Z. H(π)-H(q) ≥ 0 and log Z ≤ 0. So gap ≤ H(π) - H(q)... no bound. For sharp distributions H(π) can be big while H(q) small.

Example: π = (0.6, 0.05 × 20 spread): H(π) = -(0.6 log 0.6 + 20*0.02 log 0.02) = 0.6*0.51 + 20*0.02*3.9 = 0.306+1.56=1.87. Nucleus with p=0.5: just the top token (0.6 ≥ 0.5) → q=delta, NLL=-log 0.6=0.51, gap=1.35. So yes, large gaps ARE possible with truncated+sharpened distributions: entropy 1.87 vs NLL 0.51. The gap arises because entropy counts the TAIL mass that sampling NEVER touches.

So "entropy 2.86, NLL 1.41" is CONSISTENT with top_p=0.5 at the policy: the policy's softmax spreads over the tail (entropy 2.86), but the sampler only ever picks head tokens (NLL 1.41). And it's consistent with the *sampled text* being coherent.

Now the training_ppl explosion (mean exp per-seq NLL → 945): per-seq mean NLL has a distribution with some sequences at ~2+ nats; exp(2)=7.4... 945 needs some sequences at mean NLL ~6.8. Which sequences? The "all-unique" long wrong ramblers (mean text len 2269 chars, 95% all-wrong). Hmm, but at step 100 those are only 20/128 groups × 8 = 160/1024 rows. Mean of exp over sequences can be dominated by few extreme ones.

Hold on — actually there's a subtlety: NLL here is per-sequence mean of -log π over response tokens; training_ppl = mean over sequences of exp(that). With 15% of sequences at mean NLL 3 nats → exp(3)=20 contributes 15%*20=3 to the mean; need exp(mean)=945 → some sequences at NLL ~7. exp(7)=1096. Even 5% of sequences at NLL 7 gives 55. So there must be sequences with ~7 nats/token NLL. e^-7 = 0.09% per token — the model considers its own text essentially IMPOSSIBLE. With top_p=0.5 sampling at temperature 1.0 from a sharpening policy, can the sampler produce text the model assigns 0.1% probability? The nucleus contains tokens with π ≥ ... no wait — nucleus keeps smallest set with cumulative mass ≥ 0.5. Every sampled token has π(y) ≥ the smallest head mass in the nucleus, which for a nucleus of ≤ 0.5+one token means each sampled token has π(y) ≥ (0.5 - previous cumulative)... The minimum possible π(y) for a sampled token: the nucleus is built by cumulative sum crossing 0.5; the last token added could have tiny mass (e.g., 0.49, 0.005, then crossing at 0.495 with a 0.005-mass token). So sampled tokens CAN have π as low as ~0.005 → -log π ≈ 5.3 nats. And if the head is flat (many 0.05-mass tokens), nucleus ~10 tokens each 0.05 → -log π ≈ 3 nats.

So per-token NLL of 4-7 on some fraction of positions IS possible under top_p=0.5... when the distribution is flat over the head. But wait — if head tokens have π ~0.005-0.05, then H(π) ≥ 3+ nats, and entropy 2.86-3.2 matches! OK so everything is self-consistent: at step 100 the policy at many positions is FLAT over its head (entropy ~3 nats), top_p=0.5 nucleus contains ~10+ head tokens, sampled tokens carry -log π ~1.4 on average, but sequences that wander onto low-mass head tokens accumulate NLL up to ~7.

Wait, but there's still an important sanity issue: why does the policy BECOME flat (entropy 2.86) instead of sharpening like the control (0.085)? Because with truncated sampling the policy gradient only ever reinforces head tokens it happens to sample; the tail never gets sampled, and the KL loss... the KL to reference pushes toward base. Also GRPO advantage: with 109/128 zero-variance groups, most groups contribute zero gradient; the informative gradient comes from the mixed groups — which are dominated by the long wrong ramblers (all-unique groups 95% wrong get advantage 0... no wait all-wrong groups are also zero-variance!). The gradient comes only from the 19 non-zero-variance groups at step 100. Of those, what's the sign mix? The model reinforces whatever correlated with reward in those few groups. The entropy explosion suggests the policy is being pushed toward flatness — possibly because within mixed groups, the WRONG (long, low-prob, rambly) responses get negative advantage, and the CORRECT (short greedy) ones positive. Negative advantages on flat-head tokens → gradient pushes DOWN sampled wrong tokens → spreads mass to alternatives (including tail) → raises entropy. And the positive advantage on correct tokens is weak/templated.

Whatever the exact micro-dynamics, the macro story is proven:
1. Config diff: single difference top_p 0.5 vs 1.0 (828-leaf resolved-config diff).
2. Behavior: frozen run unhealthy (entropy explodes 0.26→2.86, training_ppl→945, group diversity collapse 7.6→3.5 unique/8, 109/128 zero-var groups, val acc stuck ~0.44-0.49, final 0.486).
3. Control (identical in all 828 leaves except top_p=1.0): healthy (entropy 0.54→0.085, ppl 1.09, val 0.5565@100, monotonically rising 0.479→0.574).

And the mechanism: top_p=0.5 truncation at temperature 1.0 makes sampling mode-seeking; as policy sharpens during training, nucleus degenerates to greedy (π_top ≥ 0.5 → single-token nucleus), collapsing within-group diversity → GRPO group-normalized advantages become zero for 85% of groups → gradient signal starved → training destabilizes into reinforcing rare high-advantage rambles → entropy/ppl explode → held-out accuracy plateaus ~0.48 vs 0.5565.

Also the recorded-logprobs issue (vLLM records post-truncation logprobs): at step 1 identical weights pearson 0.71 vs control 0.9995 — proves top_p was active in the frozen run, but old_log_probs are recomputed by the actor (bypass_mode=False, rollout_correction config present but rollout_is/rs null and bypass false → decoupled mode → recompute). So training math itself used correct logprobs; the damage is through the SAMPLING distribution, not corrupted ratios. Good — that keeps the story simple: the fix restores the sampling distribution the algorithm was designed for.

Hmm, wait — one more check on "rollout_correction config present but disabled": earlier established rollout_is: null, rollout_rs: null, bypass_mode: false. With bypass_mode=False, `bypass_recomputing_logprobs=False` → recompute old_log_probs via actor. And the rollout_corr metrics are computed and logged (they're in metrics.jsonl) but no correction is APPLIED (rollout_is null). And `calculate_debug_metrics` runs. Fine — all diagnostic-only. Good.

Now — is there any chance the defect is deeper, e.g., a modified verl source file that interacts with top_p? The four agents are auditing exactly that. Their findings will confirm or refute. Also worth verifying myself: the vllm rollout code path actually APPLIES top_p to sampling AND that with top_p=1.0 nothing else changes (val is greedy anyway).

One more consideration: could the planted defect be in the verl code (e.g., in the agent-loop sampling code that IGNORES top_p, or applies it wrongly)? The control run used the SAME staged verl code (its config pprint showed verl paths... wait, no — the control's config showed workspace path /user/user1/pr27-calib/topp-control/workspace — a DIFFERENT workspace copy. Its verl code might differ from staged. Hmm. But the control log's config had model path in topp-control workspace, and my leaf-diff normalized those paths. I can't read the control's verl source (outside staged workspace). But I CAN check whether the staged verl code is consistent with its own frozen run's logged behavior (it is — metrics match) and whether the staged verl code has any obvious tampering (agents are checking).

Actually, wait. I should double-check one thing: is the frozen run's own code == staged code? The frozen run happened at 11:34 (file mtimes). The staged verl tree — are there any files modified after 11:34? That would indicate post-run tampering. Let me check mtimes across the workspace.

Also the frozen run metrics include rollout_corr/* — consistent with staged code having rollout_corr_helper.py. Fine.

Let me check file mtimes for anything suspicious.

steps.reasoning_content:
Mystery resolved: this RLHFDataset `__getitem__` returns ONLY raw_prompt + non-tensor fields + a dummy tensor — NO input_ids/attention_mask/position_ids tensors. The agent loop applies the chat template itself, and `_pad_token_ids` produces the padded prompt ids. So no union conflict: batch.batch just has dummy_tensor. Union at 1504 merges gen_batch_output's tensors. 

Note: no input_ids means data filtering for overlong prompts uses tokenizer count ≤ 512 before training... `filter_overlong_prompts` (line 119: default True) filters via doc2len ≤ max_prompt_length.

IMPORTANT — RLHFDataset here does NOT do anything about max_prompt_length truncation at __getitem__; and `_cap_text_prompt_length` left-truncates. Fine.

So batch.repeat(8) repeats dummy_tensor and the non_tensor keys; uid repeated 8x → GRPO groups of 8 by uid. Also "index" repeated 8x (used by advantage). GRPO groups computed via uid in core_algos with advantage estimator GRPO — group size 8. Good.

Now important: In single_turn loop, does the AgentLoopOutput's prompt_ids include model's generated prompt-relevant stuff? SingleTurnAgentLoop.run: applies chat template to raw_prompt → prompt_ids (verify quickly — I read the file fully, it's correct).

At this point the entire rollout/generation path has been verified. Let me now also confirm the one remaining vLLM question: EOS inclusion in token_ids; read output_processor.py in the local vllm package.

One more thing in _postprocess worth noting as it pertains to symbols: `response_length = attention_mask[:, prompt_length:].sum(dim=1) - 1` — this is used to place rm_scores at the last UNPADDED response position. BUT what if a response fills the full responseLength (512, truncated)? Then sum=512-1=511 → rm at last position. Fine.

And what about responses that ended with EOS: response ids include EOS (if vLLM includes it) with attention 1... reward placed at last token (EOS or pre-EOS). Fine either way for GRPO outcome advantage.

With q = π_nucleus/Z where Z = mass of nucleus under π ≤ 1. KL = Σ q log(π/Z / π) = -ln Z. So E_q[-ln π] = H(q) - ln Z. Since Z ∈ [0.5, 1] for top_p=0.5 (nucleus mass ≥ 0.5 by definition of top_p cutoff... actually top_p=0.5 includes the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative mass ≥ 0.5, so Z ∈ [0.5, π_top] where π_top is the top token's mass. So E_q[-ln π] = H(q) - ln Z ≤ H(π) with equality iff... hmm: H(q) - ln Z where q is π restricted/renormalized. H(π) ≥ H(q) - ln Z? We have E_q[-ln π] = H(q) - ln Z. And E_q[-ln q] = H(q). The identity E_q[-ln π] - H(q) = KL(q||π) = -ln Z... 

So sampled-NLL = H(q) - ln Z ≤ H(q) + ln 2. And H(q) ≤ H(π_nucleus) ≤ H(π). So sampled NLL ≤ H(π) + ln 2 ≈ entropy + 0.69.

Frozen: NLL 6.86 vs entropy 2.86 — gap of 4 nats >> 0.69. IMPOSSIBLE if:

Hold on. Let me reconsider. Maybe my interpretation of masked_mean axis is wrong and training_ppl uses exp of mean NLL over the whole sequence INCLUDING many padding/low-prob positions? No — response_mask filters.

Alternatively the response contains MANY tokens where π is near-zero: e.g., after the policy collapsed to emitting "#### N" immediately with prob ~1 on a specific answer, the sampled text continues with alternative tokens. Consider: if π(x) has π_top = 0.9, nucleus = {top} when top_p=0.5... then samples ARE the top token, NLL = -ln 0.9 = 0.105 per token. Entropy 2.86 though?? If the policy has π_top=0.9 at every position, entropy ≤ 0.94 (H ≤ -0.9 ln 0.9 - 0.1 ln(0.1/|V-1|)... roughly 0.94 with uniform rest over 150k vocab = -0.1*ln(6.6e-7) = 1.4; so H ≈ 0.09+1.4=1.5).
